Welcome to your first real coding assignment in this class! Consider it an achievement making it to this first milestone :)

`dplyr` is one package in the `tidyverse`. It gives us multiple functions that make it easier to work with data. These include manipulation/transformation functions like selecting specific columns, deciding which rows to keep based on whether or not they match our conditions, and finding summary statistics for different variables and groups. Sometimes we call these steps part of “data wrangling.”

Use this assignment as an opportunity to practice applying `dplyr` for data manipulation/transformation, and also to showcase your mastery. These `dplyr` functions will be a foundation to a lot of future exploration in class.

## Load packages

The usual suspects

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse) # dplyr is contained within tidyverse
library(janitor)
```

## Read in your data

These penguins are probably becoming familiar at this point!

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins_lter.csv") # read in data

penguins <- penguins |> # clean up the names
  clean_names()

```

## 3. `filter()`

Use `filter()` to create a subset from `penguins` that only contains female penguins with a culmen length (bill length) greater than or equal to 39 millimeters, and only those that live on Dream or Torgersen islands.

Don't forget to assign to a new object name. (I'm just going to call mine `filter`)

Hints: You can always check your work using `unique()`. It'll tell you the unique values that exist in a specified column, and will also help you identify the correct spelling

```{r, messages=FALSE}
#####FOR EXCLUDING (or including??) SPECIFIC ENTRIES
#filterForQuestion3 <-
#  dplyr::filter(penguins, sex == "FEMALE", ..)

###data frame name defined first, instead of naming it within filter function
question3Filter <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::filter(
                 sex == "FEMALE",
                 culmen_length_mm >= 39,
                 island %in% c("Dream", "Torgersen")
                 )

question3Filter
```

## 4. `select()`

Starting with the `penguins` data, keep all columns except `comments`. You should have 16 total columns/variables in the end.

Assign this to a new object name so that you do not overwrite the original data!

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#####SELECT() IS SOLELY FOR COLUMNS; FOR EXCLUDING SPECIFIC COLUMNS

question4Select <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::select(-comments)

unique(question4Select)
```

## 5. `relocate()`

Starting with `penguins`, move the `individual_id` variable to the third column position, following `study_name` and `sample_number`. Use `view()` to see if it worked!

Don't forget to assign to a new object name!

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#####RELOCATE IS SOLEY FOR COLUMNS
question5Relocate <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::relocate(individual_id, .after = sample_number)

view(question5Relocate)
#####ask about why view() didn't work when running the code chunk all at once; ("Error: object 'question5Relocate' not found") was the error given in console
```

## 6. `rename()`

Starting with `penguins`, convert the `island` column to `island_name`. Use `view()` to check it worked!

Don't forget to assign to a new object name.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#####RENAME IS SOLELY FOR COLUMNS

question6Rename <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::rename(island_name = island)

view(question6Rename)
```

## 7. `mutate()`

Copy `penguins` to a new object (DATAFRAME IN THIS CASE; dataframe is a type of object) called `mutate` and add a column that displays flipper length as kilometers. Call that new column `flippometers`.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#####MUTATE ADDS NEW COLUMN

# 1 km == 1,000,000 mm
mutate <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::mutate(flippometers = flipper_length_mm * 1000000)

view(mutate)
```

## 8. `group_by() |> summarize()`

You've done this a couple times in class already!

Create a new dataframe called `number8`. Take `penguins`, group the data by island and species, then create a summary table containing the mean culmen depth (call this `culmen_depth_mean`) and mean culmen length (call this `culmen_length_mean`) for each group.

Apply `na.rm` as needed.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
###checking if na.rm is needed or not; EXCLUDES ENTRIES WITHOUT DATA
##DONE
#unique(penguins$culmen_depth_mm)
##DONE
#sum(is.na(penguins$culmen_depth_mm))
##na.rm IS NEEDED FOR CULMEN_DEPTH_MM

##DONE
# unique(penguins$culmen_length_mm)
##DONE
#sum(is.na(penguins$culmen_length_mm))
##na.rm IS NEEDED FOR CULMEN_LENGTH_MM


number8 <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::group_by(island, species) %>%
  summarize(culmen_depth_mean = mean(culmen_depth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            culmen_length_mean = mean(culmen_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
            )

view(number8)

#####ASK AS TO WHAT GROUP_BY AND SUMMARIZE ACTUALLY DOES
```

## 9. `across()`

Starting with `penguins`, only keep observations for Biscoe island, group by `species`, then use `across()` to find the maximum value for any numeric variable

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

question9Across <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::filter(island == "Biscoe") %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    across(
      c(culmen_length_mm:body_mass_g, delta_15_n_o_oo:delta_13_c_o_oo),
      max,
      na.rm = TRUE
      )
            )

view(question9Across)
```

## 10. `count()`

Starting with `penguins`, create a new object called `count` that filters out all `sex` values other than `MALE` and `FEMALE`. Then, in the same piped function, display the count of all penguins by `island`, `species`, and `sex`.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

count <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::filter(sex %in% c("MALE", "FEMALE")) %>%
  drop_na(sex) %>%        #ASK ABOUT HOW IT REMOVED THE "." ENTRIES, NOT ONLY THE NA ENTRIES; drop_na drops all non-listed entries???
  count(island, species, sex)

#total penguins are 333, which is in line with the male_female_only file, which had the same goal but for only the first half of the current question
view(count)
```

## 11. `case_when()`

Create a new object called `case_when` from `penguins` and add a new column called `size` that contains:

- "big" when `body_mass_g` is greater than or equal to 4050

- "small" when `body_mass_g` is less than 4050

Use `summary(as.factor(case_when$size))` to check your work

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# case_when <- penguins %>%
#   dplyr::mutate(size = if_else(
#                                 body_mass_g >= 4050,   #condition
#                                 "big",                 #if true
#                                 "small",               #if false
#                                 missing = "INVALID")   #invalids??
#                 )

case_when <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::mutate(size = case_when(
                                body_mass_g >= 4050 ~ "big", #if true
                                body_mass_g < 4050 ~ "small", #if false
                                is.na(body_mass_g) ~ "MISSING",   #invalids??
                                .default = "INVALID"
                                )
                )


#total is 344, which is correct; 2 invalids
summary(as.factor(case_when$size))

#########################FOR AMBER:############################
#####DIFFERENCE BETWEEN if_else(), ifelse(), AND case_when
###ifelse()
#conditional function; checks using logic/comparison (greater than, less than, etc)
#doesn't need packages loaded to function
#flexible with data types, but isn't safe/reliable; may drop "attributes", can convert types unintentionally (from user)

###if_else()
#similar to above ifelse(), but requires both outputs share exactly the same data type
#safer option due to being stricter, and also handles missing values
#fast

###case_when()
#similar to if_else() in terms of usage, but generally for 3 or more checks
#when checking conditions, stops at first match
#much more easily readable
```

## 12. Final Boss 🐧 (up to 2.5 pts extra credit)

#### OPTIONAL!!

This is meant to [*stretch*]{.underline} you, not [*stress*]{.underline} you!

You’ve made it to the Final Boss 🐧! This challenge is meant to stretch your skills and combine what you’ve learned. Take it one step at a time.

Create a new object called `final_boss` that satisfies all of the following:

1.  Start with the `penguins` dataset.

2.  Filter to keep only *female* penguins with a known `flipper_length_mm` (not `NA`) that are either on Dream or Biscoe island.

3.  Select just these columns: `species`, `island`, `flipper_length_mm`, and `body_mass_g`.

4.  Mutate a new variable called `flipper_rank`:

    - If `flipper_length_mm` is less than 190, assign `"short"`,

    - If `flipper_length_mm` is between 190 and 210, assign `"medium"`,

    - If greater than 210, assign `"long"`.

5.  Group by `species`, `island`, and `flipper_rank`, and summarize the *average body mass* (name this column `avg_mass_g`), rounded to the nearest whole number.

#### Hints:

- Use `case_when()` inside `mutate()` for flipper ranking.

- Use `round()` inside `summarize()` to round your final result.

- Your `final_boss` dataframe should be 8 observations × 4 variables.

- Use comments (`#`) to help you think through each step.

- Use `print(final_boss)` when you're done.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

final_boss <- penguins %>%
  dplyr::filter(sex == "FEMALE") %>%
###check if FEMALE Is only entry
#  unique(final_boss$sex)
  
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm) %>%
###check if there are only valid flipper lengths
#unique(final_boss$flipper_length_mm)

  filter(island %in% c("Dream", "Biscoe")) %>%
###check for only Dream and Biscoe islands
#unique(final_boss$island)
  
  select(species, island, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) %>%
###want to check column labels
#ASK HOW TO CHECK UNIQUE COLUMNS UN-MANUALLY
#don't know how to check here outside of visually/deleting all short/long entries, then checking for unique entries
  
  dplyr::mutate(flipper_rank = 
                  case_when(
                            flipper_length_mm < 190 ~ "short",
                            flipper_length_mm > 210 ~ "long",
                            is.na(flipper_length_mm) ~ "MISSING",   #invalids
                              .default = "medium" #rest should be in "medium" range
                            )
#####190 and 210 exact values were put into "medium" despite not being given an appropriate tag; ask if there is a different way to use case_when() to not default the rest of the valid values not covered by the first two conditions 
                ) %>%
  group_by(species, island, flipper_rank) %>%
  
#body mass, then get average, then round the average
  summarize(avg_mass_g = round(mean(body_mass_g)))
  #ask how to use "na.rm = TRUE" as second condition for mean to exclude missing values, since it gave an error
print(final_boss)
```
